title: The calendar of saints
hookLine: the Church's book of saints lists holy people for every day of the year

lines: A READER AT THE MORNING GATHERING.
A PLACE, A NAME, A FEW WORDS.
cards: In some monasteries, at the morning gathering, a reader stands and reads something that sounds like headlines from a very old newspaper. A place, a name, a few words about a life. At Rome, a martyr.
In Gaul, a bishop. In Egypt, a hermit. The names keep coming, from different centuries and corners of the map, and then the reading stops and the day begins.
Nobody in the room knew most of these people. Tomorrow there will be a fresh list.

teach.h: THE CHURCH'S BOOK OF SAINTS, DAY BY DAY.
teach.b: The book is the Roman Martyrology, the Church's official calendar of saints, arranged by days of the year, so that every date carries its own names.
The word martyr sits right inside it, and earlier on this climb you met that word as witness.

teach.h: TO THE UTTERMOST PART OF THE EARTH.
teach.b: So start with the job Jesus gives his friends in the Acts of the Apostles, just before he ascends, in the Douay-Rheims: "you shall be witnesses unto me in Jerusalem, and in all Judea, and Samaria, and even to the uttermost part of the earth."
Notice the map in that sentence: a city, then a region, then the ends of the earth. The Martyrology reads like that map filled in.

Tradition says the book began with those who died for their witness, and it grew to hold every kind of holy life: bishops, nurses, farmers, teachers, mothers, kings, children. The entries are short on purpose.

teach.h: A PLACE, A NAME, A LINE OR TWO.
teach.b: A place first, then a name, then a line or two. Reading it, you meet people you've never heard of, from towns you can't find, each set down as worth remembering on this exact day. The book also admits what it can't hold.
Its daily lists traditionally end by remembering the many other holy people, unnamed, whose lives only God knows. That honest gap matters.

teach.h: YOU SHALL BE WITNESSES UNTO ME.
teach.b: The Martyrology is not a hall of fame. It's a reminder that holiness is crowded, and no date on the calendar is empty of it.
The next stretch of this climb walks the year by that calendar, one saint at a time, starting with how the Church decides who goes in the book.

how: The Roman Martyrology lists saints and blesseds for each day of the year; in some monasteries and religious houses a portion is read aloud each day, and some Catholics check the day's saints in a calendar or app.

games.q: you're compiling a book of saints for each day. you run out of names you can confirm. what do you do with the rest?
o: leave the rest of the page blank.
make up a few plausible saints.
remember the many others whose names only God knows.
games.why: the Martyrology's daily lists traditionally close by remembering the many other holy people, unnamed. holiness is bigger than the list.

practice: If a Catholic calendar or a phone is near, find today's saints and read the line or two about one name you don't know. Let that stranger rest with you: where they lived, what they did with their ordinary days.
If you pray, ask that saint to pray for you; if you don't, simply hold the name, and the fact that someone remembered it.
